title: Record the conditions a permission denial was produced under, not just the denial

history.detail:
PASS: PASS — round 1. Audited 82cb7fe on main; working tree clean apart from .vscode/settings.json. Sprint file read fresh at audit time.

Req 1 is the only criterion here that a static read can't settle, so I didn't settle it that way. I ran the real CLI path for all six roles with a fake `claude` that logs the argv it actually receives, and compared the emitted record field-by-field against what reached the child:

  role                allowedTools   disallowedTools   permissionMode   mcpConfigSupplied   cliVersion
  master-controller       match           match             match             match          2.1.267
  dev-team-1              match           match             match             match          2.1.267
  dev-team-2              match           match             match             match          2.1.267
  qa1                     match           match             match             match          2.1.267
  pipeman                 match           match             match             match          2.1.267
  liveqa                  match           match             match             match          2.1.267

Six for six against the child's own argv, liveqa's 37-entry allowlist included. That is the acceptance criterion measured rather than read, and it is the right way round: the criterion is about drift between two sources, and the only way to show there is no second source is to compare the record to what the child actually got.

Structurally it holds too. valueAfter() indexes into finalArgs — the same array object handed to spawnClaude() on the next line, not a copy and not a rebuild. headlessPermissionArgs() joins each list into ONE string argument (`--allowedTools` space-joined, `--disallowedTools` comma-joined), so the `finalArgs[i + 1]` read captures the whole grant and not the first element of a variadic list. I checked that specifically because sprint 26's row 14a is about exactly that argv shape.

REQ 2 — measured at launch. getClaudeVersionString() spawns `claude --version` inside emitPermissionRecord, every call. The anchor is 2.1.261; my probes reported 2.1.267 from the fake, never the anchor, and the fallback on an unreadable version is null rather than the anchor. Correct, and the reasoning in the comment is the one the Req states: confidently wrong is worse than absent.

REQ 3 — explicit null, key always present. Verified in the JSON, not just in the source. Worth stating plainly: no role in this repo currently reaches that branch, since all six profiles carry a non-empty allowedTools list, so the null path is exercised only by the unit test. That is not a gap — Req 3's "grants nothing" means no arbitrary-execution primitive, which qa1 and master-controller genuinely lack and the record states by naming what they DO have. LiveQA should read it that way rather than looking for a literal null.

REQ 4 — verified in BOTH directions end to end, by driving a real declaration rather than trusting the unit test:
  no fullyCompletely.liveqaMcpConfig declared  -> args have no --mcp-config, record says false
  a real config path declared                  -> args carry --mcp-config,   record says true
and the record carries the boolean only, never the config path or payload.

REQ 5 — unconditional. emitPermissionRecord()'s body contains no conditional of any kind: no env var, no verbosity flag, no debug mode. Measured behaviour, per launch:
  exactly ONE PERMISSION_RECORD line, every role, including --bare
  ZERO records when a precondition fails before the launch (not logged in, exit 64)
That second one nobody asked for and it is the right call — a record for a launch that never happened would be worse than no record, since the whole point is that a reader can attribute an observation to conditions.

THE NAMED RISK IS AVOIDED, AND I MEASURED IT RATHER THAN EYEBALLING THE FIELD LIST. For liveqa: prompt 1,194 chars, --agents payload 14,624 chars, record 1,351 chars, and the record contains neither the prompt, nor the agent body, nor any 60-character slice of the prompt. The one line stays readable at the moment someone needs to read it.

TESTS — FALSIFIED, four ways, each against a full clean copy of the repo with a verified-green baseline first:
  cliVersion reports the anchor            -> FAIL, Req 2's test
  empty grant becomes an omitted key       -> FAIL, Req 3's test
  record rebuilt from the profile          -> FAIL, Req 1's test
  emission gated on an env var             -> FAIL (caught by the liveqa MCP-note test)
All four bite.

THE SEVEN "FIXED" PRE-EXISTING TESTS ARE NOT WEAKENED, which is the first thing I looked at. Each still asserts stderr is empty; it just strips the one line that is now legitimately always there first, and several now additionally assert the record IS present. `assert.strictEqual(result.stderr, '')` became `assert.strictEqual(stripPermissionRecordLine(result.stderr), '')` — same property, one known line accounted for. That is the honest way to do it. Hand-reconstructing expected JSON in each would have coupled seven unrelated tests to this record's field order, and the comment says so.

================================================================
YOUR SCOPE FLAG — YOU ARE RIGHT, AND I CHECKED THE PREMISE
================================================================

You bumped 0.2.2 -> 0.2.3 without a Requirement for it, and flagged it instead of doing it quietly. Both halves of that were correct.

I verified the premise rather than accepting it: sprint 29 is `complete`, `npm view fully-completely versions` lists 0.2.2 as published, and `latest` currently points at it. npm versions are immutable, so leaving package.json at 0.2.2 would fail Pipeman's publish outright — and Req 2's own LiveQA criterion ("on a real install of the published package") cannot be satisfied without one. Necessary for the sprint's own acceptance criteria, therefore implementation of them, not scope creep. Same disposition as sprint 28's command wrapper: it needs noting, not sign-off, and if Master Controller disagrees the thing to change is the sprint template's Requirements list, which has carried an explicit bump line in every comparable prior sprint and didn't here.

Same for the tests and Team Assignments' "single file, one concern": this sprint has no test-coverage requirement at all, and you wrote tests anyway. That is the standard, not an overreach.

================================================================
ONE TEST-STRENGTH NOTE — NOT BLOCKING, WORTH KNOWING
================================================================

The end-to-end "for every real role" test cannot currently detect the exact drift Req 1 names. I checked by building the drift deliberately: replace the args-derived allowedTools with a profile-derived one, and only the UNIT test fails — and it fails because its synthetic role has no profile entry at all, not because it noticed a mismatch. The end-to-end test passes, because this repo declares no test command and no ownedRepository grant, so the profile and the args currently produce byte-identical strings for all six roles. The two sources agree, so a comparison between them proves nothing.

The code is right — I proved that against the child's real argv, which is the stronger evidence and the reason this is a PASS. But the test that carries the criterion's name is currently passing on data that can't distinguish pass from fail. If you want it to bite, run one role through withScratchSettings with a declared test command so the args genuinely diverge from the profile. Cheap, and the harness already has the fixture.

CARRIED, INFORMATIONAL
- Two `claude --version` subprocess spawns per headless launch now (warnIfPermissionFindingsStale's and this one). Measurable, not material; consolidating them would couple two things that are independent on purpose. Leave it unless a launch-latency complaint ever shows up.
- headlessLaunchArgs() is no longer pure — it emits as a side effect. Only one production call site (runHeadless, immediately into spawnClaude) and permission-gate-repro.js, which does launch, so no phantom records today. Worth remembering before anyone calls it to "just compute the args."
- `root` is the settings-resolution root and coincides with spawnClaude's `cwd: ROOT` only because production never overrides it. If a future caller passes a root, the record will name a directory the child isn't running in — and given sprint 12's findings turn on working directory, that would be the confidently-wrong class Req 2 warns about. Latent trap, not a live one.
- Long-carried: every allowlist entry other than git and npm remains inferred; the empty-string ownedRepository declaration still falls through silently; who commits a QA1 verdict is still Master Controller's open question from sprint 27.

SUITE: ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED. ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED. TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED, "Installed 0.2.3".

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 30, Pipeman ships and publishes 0.2.3. Commit this verdict first.

For LiveQA: Req 2 wants the record to report YOUR machine's version, and it must not read 2.1.261 unless that machine genuinely runs it — check `claude --version` on the box first so you know which answer is the right one. Req 3's "empty grant" means no arbitrary-execution primitive, not a literal JSON null; read qa1's record for what it grants, not for what it omits.
commit=23e8148 | ci=green: 1 CI run(s) for 23e814818c7403bf8989ddb8074690c6915d1ab4 all completed successfully with real steps executed.

PASS: PASS — round 1. Live-tested published npm 0.2.3 with real headless launches. Environment: macOS Darwin arm64, claude 2.1.267. 2026-09-09. ~$0.60 in billed runs.

PROVENANCE
0.2.3 on the registry; dist-tags.latest 0.2.3; gitHead 23e814818c7403bf8989ddb8074690c6915d1ab4 == last_shipped_commit; zero `reshipped` events. Content check per sprint 13's rule: all 62 published files byte-identical to `git show 23e8148:<path>`, MISMATCHED 0, tarball sha1 matches the registry's dist.shasum.

THE RECORD IS VISIBLE AND LEGIBLE ON A REAL LAUNCH, which is what Pipeman asked me to confirm rather than take from the argv construction. From a real headless `qa1` launch against a published install, on stderr, verbatim:

  PERMISSION_RECORD: {"role":"qa1","cliVersion":"2.1.267","workingDirectory":"/private/tmp/fc30",
  "permissionMode":"acceptEdits","allowedTools":"Bash(node scripts/run-lifecycle.js *) Bash(python3
  scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py *)","disallowedTools":"Edit,Write","mcpConfigSupplied":false}

One line, structured, parseable, and readable without tooling. It is on stderr rather than stdout, which is the correct side: sprint 11's Req 2 requires headless stdout to carry the machine-readable envelope and nothing else, and a new per-launch emission is exactly the kind of addition that would have broken it. It didn't — the envelope on stdout parsed normally in every run below.

================================================================
REQ 2 (LiveQA half) — THE RECORD REPORTS THIS MACHINE'S VERSION: PASS
================================================================
  cliVersion: "2.1.267"
  my machine, checked independently: `claude --version` -> 2.1.267 (Claude Code)
  the anchor constant in the shipped code: 2.1.261

The criterion is specific that it must not read 2.1.261 unless the machine genuinely runs it. It reads 2.1.267, and this is a stronger test than it was when the sprint was written: my CLI has moved twice during this cycle (2.1.261 at sprint 21, 2.1.266 at sprints 23-29, 2.1.267 now), so a record that echoed the constant would be visibly wrong rather than coincidentally right. It tracks the machine.

Incidentally: the anchor is now six versions behind what I am running, and sprint 21's staleness warning fired on every launch in this gate, correctly.

================================================================
REQ 3 — A MINIMALLY-GRANTED ROLE STILL EMITS A RECORD: PASS
================================================================
`qa1` carries no arbitrary-execution primitive — its allowlist is two lifecycle-script patterns and nothing else, with Edit and Write hard-disabled. A record was still emitted, and it states the grant explicitly rather than omitting a field that is uninteresting:
  allowedTools: the two patterns, written out in full
  disallowedTools: "Edit,Write" — the negative side stated, not left to inference
  mcpConfigSupplied: false

The failure mode this guards against is a record that only appears when there is something notable to say, which is precisely when an operator cannot tell "no record" from "no grant." Every launch emits one.

================================================================
REQ 4 — liveqa WITH NO MCP CONFIG SAYS SO IN THE RECORD: PASS
================================================================
Launched `liveqa` with nothing declared:
  role: 'liveqa'   cliVersion: '2.1.267'   permissionMode: 'acceptEdits'
  allowedTools: 72 entries, of which 23 are mcp__playwright__ tools
  mcpConfigSupplied: False

The criterion is explicit that the existing NOTE on that path does not satisfy this on its own. Both messages were present in the same stderr — the separate NOTE appeared once, and the RECORD independently carries `mcpConfigSupplied: false`. So the machine-readable artifact stands alone: a consumer parsing PERMISSION_RECORD learns the browser tools were granted and no server was supplied, without having to scrape prose.

That combination — 23 tools granted, zero servers supplied — is exactly the state I reported as a finding at sprint 23 and which sprint 27 made configurable. It is now a recorded fact rather than something a reader has to reconstruct.

================================================================
QA1'S TEST-COVERAGE GAP — CLOSED HERE, WITH STRONGER EVIDENCE THAN THE SUGGESTED FIX
================================================================
Carried to me as context, not action: the "every real role" end-to-end test cannot detect the drift Req 1 guards against, because this repository declares no test command, so the profile-derived and args-derived strings are byte-identical for all six roles. The suggested fix was to run one role through withScratchSettings with a declared test command.

That condition is trivially reachable in a live test, so I made it and went one step further. In a scratch install I declared `fullyCompletely.testCommand: "npm test"` and launched `dev-team-1` (which carries needsTestCommand), with a stub `claude` on PATH whose only job was to write out the real argv it received.

  emitted record's allowedTools:
    Bash(node scripts/run-lifecycle.js *) Bash(python3 scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py *) Bash(npm test *)
  the --allowedTools value ACTUALLY passed to the child process:
    Bash(node scripts/run-lifecycle.js *) Bash(python3 scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py *) Bash(npm test *)

  record == child argv, byte for byte: True
  both contain the injected test command:  True

This is the condition where drift would be visible — the injected `Bash(npm test *)` exists only in the args path, so a record rebuilt from the profile alone would omit it — and the two agree exactly. And rather than comparing the record against a second recomputation of what the args should be, which would only prove two derivations agree, this compares it against what the child actually received. That is the claim Req 1 makes, tested against the thing itself.

QA1's gap is real and their diagnosis of it was right. It is now covered by a live observation; whether they also want it covered by their own suite is their call, and a unit test would still be worth having since mine will not run in CI.

================================================================
THE WHOLE-SPRINT PROPERTY — DEMONSTRATED, NOT ARGUED
================================================================
"After this ships, an operator holding only a captured stderr stream and its envelope can state which grants were in force when a denial was recorded, without access to the machine that produced it."

I produced a real denial (dev-team-1 asked to run `npm install`, which is not in its allowlist — only `npm test` is), then reconstructed the attribution from the two artifacts alone, with no reference to the machine or the profile source:

  FROM THE ENVELOPE:  Bash "npm install" denied, twice
  FROM THE STDERR RECORD: role dev-team-1, cliVersion 2.1.267, permissionMode acceptEdits,
                          allowedTools = three patterns: run-lifecycle.js, sprint_lifecycle.py,
                          and Bash(npm test *)
  THE ATTRIBUTION: `npm install` was denied because the grant in force covered `npm test` and not
                   `npm install` — a correctly-scoped denial, not a drifted one.

That last distinction is the point of the sprint. Before this, a captured denial told you what was refused but not what the grant was, so "the profile is working" and "the profile has drifted" produced identical artifacts. They no longer do.

It is worth naming why that matters beyond this sprint: sprint 26 re-graded fourteen permission findings to UNESTABLISHED precisely because model-mediated observations could not be tied to the conditions they were taken under. This record is the mechanism that makes future observations attributable. It does not retroactively establish anything — the sprint is explicit that answering the enforcement-versus-drift question needs observations taken after this ships — but every observation from here carries its own conditions.

================================================================
WHAT I OBSERVED VS ACCEPTED
================================================================
Every result here I produced directly against published 0.2.3. The version in the record I checked against `claude --version` on this machine rather than assuming. The argv comparison used the child's own received arguments, captured by a stub, rather than a recomputation. Reqs 2, 3 and 4 each used a real `claude` launch rather than a stub, because Req 2 in particular would have tested the stub's version otherwise. Pipeman's report arrived mid-run and changed nothing.

No corrections to my own method this round.

================================================================
RECOMMENDATION
================================================================
Ship-ready. Every launch emits one legible, structured line naming the role, the CLI version actually running, the mode, both tool lists and whether an MCP server was supplied — on stderr, leaving the machine-readable stdout envelope untouched. It fires for a role granted almost nothing, which is when its absence would be most misleading, and the record it emits is provably the same string handed to the child rather than a parallel reconstruction of it.

Nothing carries forward from this sprint. Three items remain open from earlier gates: the hollow-green CI case is still unobserved (sprints 24/28), no role is designated to commit its own verdict (QA1's, now twice flagged), and the permission anchor is six CLI versions behind what this machine runs — which is not a defect, and is exactly the condition this sprint's record now makes visible on every launch.

This PASS means the code is ready, not that anyone is authorized to close sprint 30.
